text: Lesson 18 covered what gets found. This lesson covers the real tools that find it at cloud scale: Microsoft Defender for Cloud on the Azure side, and AWS Security Hub on the AWS side. Both exist to solve the same underlying problem -- nobody can manually check thousands of resources against a security baseline every day -- but each one does it with its own native services and its own way of presenting the result.

Microsoft Defender for Cloud is Azure's native CSPM tool, combined with workload protection for the resources it's actively watching. Its signature output is the Secure Score: a single percentage that summarizes how well an environment currently matches the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark, built from the specific recommendations it's generated -- like the public-storage and open-security-group findings from Lesson 18. Despite the name, Defender for Cloud isn't limited to Azure; it can also connect to and assess AWS and GCP accounts from the same dashboard.

AWS Security Hub plays a similar role on the AWS side, but it works by aggregation rather than scanning everything itself. AWS already has dedicated services doing specific jobs -- GuardDuty for threat detection, Inspector for vulnerability scanning, Macie for sensitive-data discovery, IAM Access Analyzer for permission checks -- and Security Hub pulls their findings, plus findings from supported third-party tools, into one consolidated view. It then checks that combined picture against recognized standards like the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark and the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, producing a compliance score per standard.

Strip away the branding and both tools are doing the same three things: aggregating findings from wherever security data already exists, checking those findings against a recognized baseline, and compressing the result into a score a team can actually track over time instead of staring at a raw list of hundreds of findings.

Defender for Cloud and Security Hub both end in the same place -- a score. Lesson 20 picks up from there: what that compliance score actually represents, and the real workflow a team follows to turn one finding into a confirmed fix.
